analysis.one_liner: Guarantees immigrants in CBP or ICE custody access to a lawyer, food, water, and restrooms.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote; it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law that anyone facing deportation, exclusion, or an immigration inspection has the right to a lawyer of their choosing. If someone is held at a border port of entry or in a Customs and Border Protection or Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility and cannot meet a lawyer in person, the agency would have to set up remote communication with counsel from the first hour of detention onward. Someone denied access to a lawyer could not be pressed into signing paperwork giving up their green card or withdrawing their request to enter the country. The bill would also require that any holding be as short and least restrictive as practicable, and that detainees have access to food, water, and restrooms.
analysis.who_benefits: People held at ports of entry or in CBP and ICE detention facilities— asylum seekers, lawful permanent residents re-entering the country, and others facing removal proceedings—would gain enforceable rights to counsel, remote lawyer contact within the first hour of detention, protection from signing away their status without counsel, and minimum conditions of food, water, and restrooms.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the right to counsel of one's choosing to every removal, exclusion, deportation, or inspection proceeding, where current law only guarantees it in removal proceedings [S2][S3].
Requires CBP or ICE to provide a way for a lawyer to communicate remotely with a detained person during the first hour and thereafter of detention, at any time of day [S3].

Bars a detained person from submitting a valid form abandoning lawful permanent resident status or withdrawing an application for admission if they were denied access to counsel—closing a pathway in which people at ports of entry sign away their rights under pressure [S2][S3].
Requires that holding or detention be limited to the briefest term and least restrictive conditions practicable, and include access to food, water, and restroom facilities [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government—CBP and ICE—would bear the cost of operating facilities that meet the minimum conditions and of providing remote counsel-communication options around the clock. The bill does not require the government to pay for detainees' lawyers themselves; it removes the current statutory language stating representation is at no expense to the government, leaving detainees to pay their own counsel or rely on pro bono lawyers [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Requiring agencies to enable lawyer contact within the first hour of any holding, at any hour, and to guarantee food, water, and restroom access at ports of entry would impose real operational costs and logistics burdens on border facilities that are often crowded and rapidly processing large numbers of people [S3].

The bill leaves the cost of legal representation with detainees or volunteer lawyers; it does not create a government-funded right to counsel, so many detained people would still lack a lawyer in practice [S2][S3].

Opponents of expanding rights for people in immigration custody argue that easier counsel access and shorter, less restrictive detention could slow border processing and complicate enforcement; the bill text and summary do not address these enforcement concerns [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are modest but concrete: a right to contact a lawyer quickly, a safeguard against signing away legal status without counsel, and minimum standards of food, water, and restrooms. The main costs fall on federal agencies' operations rather than on ordinary taxpayers directly, though the bill does not fund lawyers for detainees, which limits how much it would change in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Kamala Harris introduced the bill on July 23, 2019, joined by six Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
No further action was ever recorded—no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote—so the bill expired at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal immigration agencies—CBP and ICE—kept the discretion to run ports of entry and detention facilities under existing rules, without the new counsel-access and condition requirements. Detained immigrants remained under the prior, weaker statutory protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Immigration agencies kept current detention practices

for.name: Sen. Kamala Harris
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend counsel-access and detention-condition protections to people held by CBP and ICE.

for.name: 6 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Blumenthal, Warren, Gillibrand, Markey, Merkley, and one other)

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lindsey Graham (R)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred—no hearing, markup, or vote—leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no opposition is on the record; the sponsor and all six cosponsors were Democrats, and the Senate had a Republican majority whose committee did not act.

industries.note: Companies that operate ICE detention facilities under contract would face a legal requirement to keep detentions as short and least restrictive as practicable and to provide food, water, and restrooms, which could reduce detention populations and per-bed revenue [S3]. Their interest in prolonged detention runs against the protections this bill gives detainees.

The bill expands the right to counsel to inspections and exclusion proceedings and guarantees remote lawyer contact during detention, creating more opportunities for attorneys to represent detained people—many of whom currently face counsel access barriers at ports of entry [S2][S3].
